messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 68
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: African
  relationship_status: Widowed
  occupation: Policy Analyst
  trauma_type: Life-threatening illness
  pcl5: 77

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Threat: Concentration: Having difficulty concentrating, Body on Alert: My body feels constantly tense and ready to react to danger, Alert at Home: I feel on guard even inside my own home
  Memory: Emotionless Recall: Sometimes I can recall what happened but feel completely numb, as if it happened to a stranger, Feels Present Not Past: The memory feels like it is happening right now rather than something that is over, Overwhelm on Recall: When the memory returns I feel so overwhelmed by emotion that I have to stop
  Negative Appraisals: Lost Emotions: I will never be able to feel normal emotions again, Body as Enemy: My body keeps reacting as if I am still in danger even when I am safe, Body Unreliable: I can no longer trust my own body

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Threat
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Memory → Threat
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Kwame is a 68-year-old widowed Ghanaian-American man who works as a senior policy analyst for a federal health agency in Washington, D.C. He was referred for psychological assessment following a prolonged hospitalisation eighteen months ago, during which he was placed in an intensive care unit for three weeks after a sudden cardiac arrest that left him clinically dead for several minutes before resuscitation. He had been preparing a briefing document at his desk when the event occurred — colleagues found him slumped in his chair, unresponsive — and the first responders who arrived described the scene to him later in terms he has never been able to forget. He has a PCL-5 score of 77, placing him in a range consistent with severe post-traumatic stress, and he presents to the current clinic having exhausted what he describes as his own private attempts to manage.

In the weeks following his discharge, Kwame returned to work earlier than his cardiologist advised, partly because the structure of the office felt safer than the silence of the home he had shared with his late wife. He told himself the worst was over. But the memory of the cardiac event did not behave as a past thing. It returned not as recollection but as re-occurrence — a sensation of the chest tightening, the sudden darkness, the absence of breath — and when it did, it felt to Kwame with full physiological conviction that it was happening right now rather than something that is over. These intrusive returns were not always overwhelming; sometimes he could recall the sequence of events with an almost clinical detachment, as though it had happened to a stranger, the emotional content drained entirely from the images. But at other times the memory arrived with such force that he had to stop whatever he was doing — mid-sentence in a briefing, mid-paragraph in a policy draft — simply to survive the wave of it.

The memory's unpredictability began to reshape how Kwame moved through his days. Because the intrusions carried such vivid physical immediacy, he had come to believe that his body could not be trusted to distinguish between danger and safety. Each time the memory returned with its full sensory weight, his nervous system responded as though the arrest were recurring, and this physiological response — the racing pulse, the muscular bracing, the inability to draw a full breath — confirmed for him that his body was still in danger even when no external threat existed. He was certain, in a way that felt empirical rather than fearful, that his body had become an unreliable instrument, prone to betrayal without warning. This belief kept him in a state of constant physical vigilance: his body felt perpetually tense and primed, and he remained on guard even inside his own apartment, scanning for the internal signal that would tell him something was wrong.

The appraisals themselves fed the threat system in a way that was difficult to interrupt. Because Kwame interpreted every somatic fluctuation — a missed heartbeat, a moment of breathlessness after climbing stairs — as evidence that his body was again failing him, the perceived threat never fully receded. This sustained sense of danger in turn made the traumatic memory more accessible, more easily triggered, and harder to contextualise as past. At his desk in the agency's open-plan office, the particular quality of fluorescent light and the ambient sound of keyboards had become potent retrieval cues — close enough to the sensory texture of that afternoon to pull the memory forward. The intrusions then reinforced his conviction that his body was operating outside his control, which deepened the threat appraisal, which kept his nervous system mobilised, which made the next intrusion more likely.

Over the past year, concentration has become genuinely impaired — he loses the thread of complex policy arguments mid-analysis, something that was never true of him before — and he has begun to fear that even his professional competence is eroding. What frightened him most, and what finally brought him to seek help, was the growing sense that he would never be able to feel normal emotions again — that the numbness he sometimes felt during recall was not a phase but a permanent condition, the emotional life he had shared with his wife now doubly inaccessible. He arrived at the first session quiet and precise, carrying a folder of his own notes. He hoped, he said, to understand what was happening inside him. He was not sure he believed it could be changed.
